case_info.scenario: A 12-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented with a left maxillary gingival swelling of 4 years’ duration associated with palatal tipping of the left maxillary central incisor. The lesion reportedly grew over a 2-year period but remained unchanged over the past 2 years. The patient denied pain, bleeding, or neurosensory disturbances associated with the lesion or dentition. Intraoral examination was notable for a firm, 1 × 1-cm, pink, dome-shaped gingival mass extending onto the facial surface of tooth number 9, coalescing with a broader, pale-appearing, soft to firm gingival enlargement apical to the tooth (Figure, A). No edema, erythema, or signs of infection were appreciated, and the adjacent teeth demonstrated no mobility with normal periodontal probing depths and vitality. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Radiographic examination showed no endodontic involvement or intralesional calcifications; however, cone-beam computed tomography imaging revealed saucerization of the facial bone near tooth number 9. Excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed, and microscopic examination of multiple sections revealed a nodule of keratinized superficial stratified squamous epithelium overlying fibrous connective tissue (Figure, B). The surface epithelium demonstrated a normal maturational pattern. The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). Small basophilic spherical calcifications were intermixed with the odontogenic epithelium.

case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

B, Low-power histomicrograph shows a nodule of fibrous connective tissue surfaced by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (original magnification ×5). The bulk of the specimen consists of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles with scattered fibroblasts. Centrally, there is a focal proliferation of odontogenic epithelium (pink arrowhead). The inset shows a higher-power image with a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of hyperchromatic ovoid cells that are arranged into pseudoductal structures (blue arrowheads; original magnification ×20). Small basophilic calcifications also are identified within the epithelial proliferation (black arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Intraoral examination was notable for a firm, 1 × 1-cm, pink, dome-shaped gingival mass extending onto the facial surface of tooth number 9, coalescing with a broader, pale-appearing, soft to firm gingival enlargement apical to the tooth (Figure, A). No edema, erythema, or signs of infection were appreciated, and the adjacent teeth demonstrated no mobility with normal periodontal probing depths and vitality. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Radiographic examination showed no endodontic involvement or intralesional calcifications; however, cone-beam computed tomography imaging revealed saucerization of the facial bone near tooth number 9. Excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed, and microscopic examination of multiple sections revealed a nodule of keratinized superficial stratified squamous epithelium overlying fibrous connective tissue (Figure, B). The surface epithelium demonstrated a normal maturational pattern. The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). Small basophilic spherical calcifications were intermixed with the odontogenic epithelium.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: A 12-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented with a left maxillary gingival swelling of 4 years’ duration associated with palatal tipping of the left maxillary central incisor. The lesion reportedly grew over a 2-year period but remained unchanged over the past 2 years. The patient denied pain, bleeding, or neurosensory disturbances associated with the lesion or dentition. Intraoral examination was notable for a firm, 1 × 1-cm, pink, dome-shaped gingival mass extending onto the facial surface of tooth number 9, coalescing with a broader, pale-appearing, soft to firm gingival enlargement apical to the tooth (Figure, A). No edema, erythema, or signs of infection were appreciated, and the adjacent teeth demonstrated no mobility with normal periodontal probing depths and vitality. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Radiographic examination showed no endodontic involvement or intralesional calcifications; however, cone-beam computed tomography imaging revealed saucerization of the facial bone near tooth number 9. Excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed, and microscopic examination of multiple sections revealed a nodule of keratinized superficial stratified squamous epithelium overlying fibrous connective tissue (Figure, B). The surface epithelium demonstrated a normal maturational pattern. The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). Small basophilic spherical calcifications were intermixed with the odontogenic epithelium.
case_info.caption: A, Large, rounded submucosal lesion of the anterior maxilla facial and apical to tooth number 9. B, Low-power histomicrograph shows a nodule of fibrous connective tissue surfaced by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (original magnification ×5). The bulk of the specimen consists of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles with scattered fibroblasts. Centrally, there is a focal proliferation of odontogenic epithelium (pink arrowhead). The inset shows a higher-power image with a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of hyperchromatic ovoid cells that are arranged into pseudoductal structures (blue arrowheads; original magnification ×20). Small basophilic calcifications also are identified within the epithelial proliferation (black arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.
